Now, technical and design decisions first. Let's think:
1. For the Capabilities Framework (U1): We will implement the three separate capability maps (root channel, application, orderer) as specified, with only V1.1 capability per map for v1.1. We will enforce crash for binaries that don't support required capabilities, no graceful fallback for v1.1 as per spec. Orderer capability enforcement will be implemented to prevent application group enabling capabilities before orderer group is upgraded, to avoid forks.
2. For U2 (RYW): The GetTrxState API will be added to the chaincode shim interface, with a boolean flag to enable RYW per transaction, backed by transient data store for the active transaction's writes.
3. For U3: The guide will be a 5-minute video with accompanying slide deck, covering pre-requisites, step-by-step config changes, and verification steps, no network downtime required as per spec.
4. For U4: Performance testing will use standard Fabric benchmark workloads (e.g., 1000 concurrent query transactions against CouchDB with 10k documents) and report p50/p95 latency and throughput.
5. For U5: MSPConfig will be converted to an interface with a default implementation matching existing configtxgen behavior, to allow custom implementations without breaking existing tooling.
6. For U6: All chaincode singletons (e.g., global chaincode metadata, deployment singletons) will be refactored to be instance-scoped, with no changes to public chaincode shim API to avoid breaking existing chaincode.
7. For U7: The test config generator will use a World struct (defined in test framework) to template core.yaml and orderer.yaml, with all existing config parameters supported, no changes to production config parsing.
8. For U8: The validation interface will return chaincode validation parameters (endorsement policy, version) and for +lifecycle will return a default majority endorsement policy, with support for channel config policies as a future extension noted in code.

Now assumptions, let's list those:
1. All existing Fabric component codebases (peer, orderer, SDK, CA) are available in the development environment, with existing CI/CD pipelines for testing.
2. The Capabilities Framework changes will be integrated with existing channel config update logic, no need to rewrite config update transaction processing from scratch.
3. For U2, RYW will only be supported for CouchDB state database (as LevelDB does not support transactional reads of uncommitted writes), which is an acceptable limitation for v1.1.
4. For U3, the video and guide will be targeted at Fabric network administrators with basic familiarity with Fabric config transactions, no need for beginner-level content.
5. For U4, CouchDB performance testing will be run on a single-node CouchDB instance (not clustered) as that is the most common deployment for small to medium Fabric networks.
6. For U5, existing configtxgen tool will continue to use the default MSPConfig implementation, no changes required to configtxgen functionality.
7. For U6, the singleton removal will not change the external behavior of chaincode deployment and invocation, only internal testability and lifecycle management.
8. For U7, the World config will be a Go struct in the existing Fabric test framework, with all existing test configuration parameters mapped to it.
9. For U8, the validation interface will be implemented in the new lifecycle system, with no changes to the existing v1.0 lifecycle system.

technical_and_design_decisions: The Capabilities Framework will use three separate capability maps (root channel, application, orderer) as specified, with only the V1.1 capability defined per map for the v1.1 release to minimize capability proliferation.

For v1.1, binaries that do not support required channel capabilities will crash immediately on startup or config update, with no graceful fallback, to ensure data integrity and provide clear administrative feedback.
The orderer will enforce that orderer group capabilities are enabled before application group capabilities can be enabled, to prevent blockchain forks during the initial v1.1 upgrade.

The RYW (Read Your Writes) feature will be implemented via a new GetTrxState method in the chaincode shim, with per-transaction enablement, and will be limited to CouchDB state database due to LevelDB's lack of support for uncommitted transactional reads.
MSPConfig will be converted to an interface with a default implementation that preserves existing configtxgen behavior, to avoid breaking existing tooling while enabling custom config generation.
Chaincode singletons will be refactored to instance-scoped without changes to the public chaincode shim API, to preserve backward compatibility for existing chaincode.
The test config generator for peer core.yaml and orderer.yaml will use a World struct in the existing Fabric test framework, with no changes to production config parsing logic.

The new lifecycle validation interface will include a special case for the +lifecycle system chaincode to return a default majority endorsement policy, with a stub for future support of channel config policies as endorsement policies.
assumptions: All existing Hyperledger Fabric component codebases (peer, orderer, SDK, CA) and CI/CD pipelines are available in the development environment, with no need for custom environment setup beyond standard onboarding.
The Capabilities Framework changes will integrate with existing channel config update processing logic, with no need to rewrite core config transaction handling from scratch.
The RYW feature is only required to work with CouchDB state database for the v1.1 release, as LevelDB support is not a requirement for this increment.

The org addition training materials (video and guide) are targeted at Fabric network administrators with basic familiarity with Fabric configuration and config transactions, so no beginner-level content is required.
CouchDB performance testing will be conducted on a single-node CouchDB deployment, which is the most common configuration for small to medium Fabric networks.
The existing configtxgen tool will continue to use the default MSPConfig implementation, so no changes to configtxgen functionality are required beyond updating it to use the new interface.
The removal of chaincode singletons will not alter the external behavior of chaincode deployment, invocation, or the public chaincode shim API, only internal implementation and testability.

The World test config struct will be added to the existing Fabric test framework, with all existing test configuration parameters mapped to its fields, and no changes to production configuration code.
The new lifecycle validation interface will be implemented only for the new lifecycle system, with no changes required to the existing v1.0 lifecycle system.
